title: Pots of honey, still good, sealed in tombs thousands of years old.
description:
Pots of honey, still good, sealed in tombs thousands of years old. Ancient Egyptian tombs in particular have turned up jars of honey that are millennia old and, once opened, still edible.

Raw nectar is mostly water. Finished honey barely is. Bees fan the nectar with their wings until most of the moisture is gone, leaving too little water for bacteria to get a foothold.

Honey is acidic, and it makes its own disinfectant. A pH of roughly 3 to 4.5 already kills off most microbes. An enzyme from the bees' own stomachs adds hydrogen peroxide on top, the same compound used to clean wounds.

Honey has been medicine for thousands of years. The earliest written use is on Sumerian clay tablets, where honey appears in roughly three in ten prescriptions. Egyptian physicians used it as a wound and eye ointment, because nothing could grow on it long enough to cause an infection.

It only works sealed. Crack the jar and let the damp in, and even honey can finally spoil.

Sources:
- https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/the-science-behind-honeys-eternal-shelf-life-1218690/ - Smithsonian Magazine (Natasha Geiling, 22 August 2013), read in full, quoting Amina Harris, executive director of the Honey and Pollination Center at the Robert Mondavi Institute, UC Davis, throughout. Established that archaeologists have repeatedly found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs, thousands of years old and still preserved; that honey is hygroscopic and bees actively dry the nectar, which starts at 60 to 80 per cent water, by flapping their wings, leaving too little moisture for microbes to survive; that honey's pH sits at roughly 3 to 4.5, acidic enough to kill off almost anything trying to grow in it; that bees carry an enzyme, glucose oxidase, which mixes with the nectar during regurgitation into the comb and produces gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide, adding further antimicrobial power; that the earliest recorded medicinal use of honey is on Sumerian clay tablets, where it appears in roughly 30 per cent of prescriptions, and that ancient Egyptian physicians used honey ointments on skin and eye conditions because nothing could grow on an open wound covered in it; and that the preservation holds only while the jar stays sealed, since added water or an open lid can let it spoil after all.
